RIGHT OF PUBLICITY DEMAND LETTER INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Media LLC

PURPOSE OF THIS RIGHT OF PUBLICITY LETTER
This letter is sent by Jordan Alex Lee to Acme Media LLC concerning use of Taylor Morgan's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness. Jordan Alex Lee is sending this letter to describe Jordan Alex Lee's concerns and to request specific actions in response, by no later than October 15, 2026. This information sheet describes California's statutory right of publicity under Civil Code sections 3344 and 3344.1. California courts have also recognized a related common-law right of publicity, distinct from these statutes; this information sheet addresses only the statutory framework and does not separately source or describe the common-law claim's elements.

DESCRIPTION OF THE IDENTITY AT ISSUE AND THE CONDUCT AT ISSUE
Jordan Alex Lee identifies the name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness at issue as follows: photograph and name, belonging to Taylor Morgan.

Based on information currently available to Jordan Alex Lee, the following describes conduct that Jordan Alex Lee believes may involve use of Taylor Morgan's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness without consent: used in a paid social media advertisement without consent

This description reflects Jordan Alex Lee's current understanding. It is not a judicial finding, and nothing in this letter states that a court has determined that any violation of Taylor Morgan's rights under California Civil Code section 3344, section 3344.1, or any other law has occurred.

CALIFORNIA'S STATUTORY RIGHT OF PUBLICITY: THE KNOWING-USE STANDARD AND STATUTORY REMEDIES FOR LIVING PERSONS
California's principal right-of-publicity statute creates civil liability for any person who knowingly uses another's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, in any manner, on or in products, merchandise, or goods, or for purposes of advertising or selling, or soliciting purchases of, products, merchandise, goods, or services, without that person's prior consent (or, for a minor, the prior consent of a parent or legal guardian). The statute's own text requires a "knowing" use — it is not a strict-liability standard that reaches an innocent or unaware use. Where liability is established, the statute sets the injured party's recovery at the greater of $750 or the person's actual damages, and separately allows recovery of any profits from the unauthorized use that are not already counted in that actual-damages figure — meaning the statutory floor and the disgorgement-of-profits remedy are cumulative with each other, not alternatives a plaintiff must choose between. The statute places the burden of proving gross revenue attributable to the use on the injured party, and the burden of proving deductible expenses on the person who violated the statute. Punitive damages may also be awarded. Separately, the statute makes the prevailing party in any action under this section entitled to attorney's fees and costs — a mandatory, prevailing-party fee-shifting rule that is not limited to a prevailing plaintiff and does not depend on a discretionary "exceptional case" finding of the kind this tool's Trademark Infringement Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet describes for federal trademark claims.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person who knowingly uses another’s name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, in any manner, on or in products, merchandise, or goods, or for purposes of advertising or selling, or soliciting purchases of, products, merchandise, goods, or services, without that person’s prior consent, or, in the case of a minor, the prior consent of their parent or legal guardian, shall be liable for any damages sustained by the person or persons injured as a result thereof."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, right of publicity — knowing-use standard for living persons (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3344.)
  "the person who violated the section shall be liable to the injured party or parties in an amount equal to the greater of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or the actual damages suffered by them as a result of the unauthorized use, and any profits from the unauthorized use that are attributable to the use and are not taken into account in computing the actual damages. In establishing these profits, the injured party or parties are required to present proof only of the gross revenue attributable to the unauthorized use, and the person who violated this section is required to prove their deductible expenses. Punitive damages may also be awarded to the injured party or parties. The prevailing party in any action under this section shall also be entitled to attorney’s fees and costs."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, statutory damages, profits, punitive damages, and prevailing-party attorney's fees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3344.)

Both citations below are to the same statutory subdivision, Section 3344(a)(1); they are quoted as two separate passages because they address two distinct topics within that one subdivision — the conduct the statute prohibits, and the remedies available for it — not because they are independent corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness violates Section 3344 or any other right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter.

A 2025 AMENDMENT: INJUNCTIONS, TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDERS, AND A TWO-BUSINESS-DAY COMPLIANCE WINDOW
In addition to the damages, profits, punitive-damages, and attorney's-fee remedies described elsewhere in this document, California's statute separately allows a party to seek an injunction or temporary restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure section 527. The statute further provides that if a court grants an order under Code of Civil Procedure section 527(c) requiring the respondent to remove, recall, or otherwise cease the publication or distribution of the petitioner's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, the respondent must complete that removal, recall, or cessation within two business days of being served with the order, unless the order itself states otherwise. This injunctive-relief provision was added to the statute by a 2025 amendment effective January 1, 2026, and is current law as of the date this clause was checked.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In addition to the remedies available in paragraph (1), a party may seek an injunction or temporary restraining order pursuant to Section 527 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If the court grants the applicant an order under subdivision (c) of Section 527 of the Code of Civil Procedure that requires the respondent to remove, recall, or otherwise cease the publication or distribution of the petitioner’s name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, the respondent shall complete the removal or recall, or cease the publication or distribution, within two business days from the day the order is served, unless otherwise required by the order."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, injunction/TRO remedy and two-business-day compliance window (2025 amendment, effective January 1, 2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3344.)

This clause cites a single statutory subdivision; no additional independent source was needed for it. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness violates Section 3344 or any other right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter or seek any injunction or restraining order from any court.

STATUTORY EXCEPTIONS: NEWS AND POLITICAL USE, COMMERCIAL-MEDIUM SPONSORSHIP, AND THE INNOCENT-PUBLISHER EXEMPTION
California's living-person right-of-publicity statute contains three distinct, narrow carve-outs, rather than one general exemption. First, a use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness in connection with any news, public affairs, or sports broadcast or account, or any political campaign, is not a use for which consent is required. Second, use in a commercial medium is not automatically exempt merely because the material containing the use is commercially sponsored or contains paid advertising — the statute makes this a question of fact, turning on whether the use was so directly connected with the commercial sponsorship or paid advertising as to itself require consent. Third, the statute exempts the owners or employees of an advertising medium (the statute's own examples include newspapers, magazines, radio and television networks and stations, cable television systems, billboards, and transit ads) who publish or disseminate someone else's violating advertisement or solicitation, unless it is established that those owners or employees had knowledge of the unauthorized use — an innocent-publisher defense that runs to the medium, not to the person who created the unauthorized use. None of these three provisions is the same as the "single and original work of fine art" language that appears in California's separate posthumous right-of-publicity statute, addressed in another clause of this document; the living-person statute does not contain that specific phrase.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, news, public affairs, sports, and political-campaign exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3344.)
  "The use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness in a commercial medium shall not constitute a use for which consent is required under subdivision (a) solely because the material containing the use is commercially sponsored or contains paid advertising. Rather it shall be a question of fact whether or not the use of the person’s name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness was so directly connected with the commercial sponsorship or with the paid advertising as to constitute a use for which consent is required under subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, commercial-medium sponsorship — question of fact, not automatic exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3344.)
  "Nothing in this section shall apply to the owners or employees of any medium used for advertising, including, but not limited to, newspapers, magazines, radio and television networks and stations, cable television systems, billboards, and transit ads, by whom any advertisement or solicitation in violation of this section is published or disseminated, unless it is established that those owners or employees had knowledge of the unauthorized use of the person’s name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness as prohibited by this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, innocent-publisher exemption for advertising media (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3344.)

This clause cites three subdivisions of the same statutory section, Cal. Civ. Code § 3344 — subdivisions (d), (e), and (f) — and they are not independent sources; all three are grouped together here because they together describe the statute's own exceptions to the consent requirement, not because they corroborate one another. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness violates Section 3344 or any other right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter.

THE POSTHUMOUS RIGHT OF PUBLICITY UNDER SECTION 3344.1: THE SAME REMEDIES, BUT NO 'KNOWING USE' REQUIREMENT IN THE STATUTORY TEXT
California has a separate statute addressing the right of publicity of a deceased personality. Its liability standard tracks the living-person statute in most respects — a person who uses a deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, in any manner, on or in products, merchandise, or goods, or for purposes of advertising or selling, or soliciting purchases of, products, merchandise, goods, or services, without prior consent from the statutorily specified person or persons, is liable, with the same remedy structure: the greater of $750 or actual damages, plus profits not already counted in actual damages, potential punitive damages, and prevailing-party attorney's fees and costs. But comparing the two sections' actual text side by side reveals a real difference: the living-person statute's operative sentence begins "Any person who knowingly uses...," while the posthumous statute's operative sentence begins "a person who uses a deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness... without prior consent... shall be liable" — with no "knowingly" or other knowledge qualifier appearing in that sentence. On the statutory text alone, the posthumous claim is not conditioned on the same knowing-use language that the living-person claim's own text requires.

THE POSTHUMOUS RIGHT'S 70-YEAR DURATION, STATUTORY SUCCESSORS, AND THE SECRETARY OF STATE REGISTRATION REQUIREMENT
California's posthumous right-of-publicity statute is time-limited: an action may not be brought under the statute by reason of any use of a deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness occurring after the expiration of 70 years after the death of the deceased personality. The statute vests these rights, after death, in specified persons and allows the right to be exercised, on behalf of and for the benefit of all of them, by those who together hold more than a one-half interest — the statute's own formula then allocates that interest among a surviving spouse, surviving children and grandchildren, or surviving parents, depending on who survives the deceased personality. The statute also conditions a successor-in-interest's or licensee's ability to recover damages on registration: a successor in interest or licensee may not recover damages for a use that occurs before that person registers a claim of rights with the California Secretary of State, on a prescribed, verified form that must include the deceased personality's name and date of death, the claimant's name and address, the basis of the claim, and the rights claimed.

THE POSTHUMOUS STATUTE'S ENTERTAINMENT-WORK AND SINGLE-AND-ORIGINAL-WORK-OF-ART EXEMPTION
California's posthumous right-of-publicity statute contains an exemption with no identically worded counterpart in the living-person statute described elsewhere in this document. A play, book, magazine, newspaper, musical composition, audiovisual work, radio or television program, single and original work of art, work of political or newsworthy value, or an advertisement or commercial announcement for any of these works, is not considered a "product, article of merchandise, good, or service" under the statute if it is fictional or nonfictional entertainment, or a dramatic, literary, or musical work — meaning a deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness used within such a work generally falls outside the conduct the statute otherwise reaches. The statute narrows that exemption, however, for a use within such a work that functions as advertising: if the work includes a use connected with a product, article of merchandise, good, or service, that specific use is not exempt if the claimant proves it is so directly connected with the product, article of merchandise, good, or service as to constitute an act of advertising, selling, or soliciting purchases of it by the deceased personality without the required consent. In other words, the exemption protects the work itself but does not extend to a merchandising or advertising use embedded within an otherwise-exempt work.

A 2024 AMENDMENT: THE DIGITAL REPLICA PROVISION FOR AI-GENERATED VOICE OR LIKENESS OF A DECEASED PERSONALITY
A 2024 amendment to California's posthumous right-of-publicity statute, effective January 1, 2025, added a separate liability provision aimed at AI-generated "digital replicas." A person who produces, distributes, or makes available the digital replica of a deceased personality's voice or likeness in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording, without prior consent from the statutorily specified person or persons, is liable to the injured party in an amount equal to the greater of $10,000 or actual damages — a statutory minimum substantially higher than the $750 minimum that applies under the statute's general provision described elsewhere in this document. The statute defines "digital replica" as a computer-generated, highly realistic electronic representation, readily identifiable as an individual's voice or visual likeness, embodied in a sound recording, image, audiovisual work, or transmission, where the individual either did not actually perform or appear, or did perform or appear but the fundamental character of that performance or appearance has been materially altered; the definition expressly excludes ordinary electronic reproduction, sampling, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering that the copyright holder has authorized. The statute also lists specific circumstances in which a digital replica may be used without consent, including use connected with news, public affairs, or sports broadcasts; use for comment, criticism, scholarship, satire, or parody; a documentary or historical or biographical representation of the individual as themselves (unless intended to, and actually does, create the false impression of an authentic recording); and fleeting or incidental use.

expectedJSON.body: California's living-person right-of-publicity statute contains three distinct, narrow carve-outs, rather than one general exemption. First, a use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness in connection with any news, public affairs, or sports broadcast or account, or any political campaign, is not a use for which consent is required. Second, use in a commercial medium is not automatically exempt merely because the material containing the use is commercially sponsored or contains paid advertising — the statute makes this a question of fact, turning on whether the use was so directly connected with the commercial sponsorship or paid advertising as to itself require consent. Third, the statute exempts the owners or employees of an advertising medium (the statute's own examples include newspapers, magazines, radio and television networks and stations, cable television systems, billboards, and transit ads) who publish or disseminate someone else's violating advertisement or solicitation, unless it is established that those owners or employees had knowledge of the unauthorized use — an innocent-publisher defense that runs to the medium, not to the person who created the unauthorized use. None of these three provisions is the same as the "single and original work of fine art" language that appears in California's separate posthumous right-of-publicity statute, addressed in another clause of this document; the living-person statute does not contain that specific phrase.

The statute vests these rights, after death, in specified persons and allows the right to be exercised, on behalf of and for the benefit of all of them, by those who together hold more than a one-half interest — the statute's own formula then allocates that interest among a surviving spouse, surviving children and grandchildren, or surviving parents, depending on who survives the deceased personality. The statute also conditions a successor-in-interest's or licensee's ability to recover damages on registration: a successor in interest or licensee may not recover damages for a use that occurs before that person registers a claim of rights with the California Secretary of State, on a prescribed, verified form that must include the deceased personality's name and date of death, the claimant's name and address, the basis of the claim, and the rights claimed.

In other words, the exemption protects the work itself but does not extend to a merchandising or advertising use embedded within an otherwise-exempt work.
